intro_html:
This page holds the real exam material: the 2025 and 2024 midterm papers, their exhibits at full size, and both answer keys, followed by the course readings and slides the papers draw on. Red highlights mark traps: wording that changes what is asked, a log axis, a mark the key gives for a step most people skip. Yellow highlights explain what a line means in course terms and where it goes in your answer. Every note links back to the matching section of the prep page.

In the week before the exam, write each paper cold first, on the prep page with the answers hidden. Prof. Cornelson's advice on Canvas: “I HIGHLY recommend that you attempt the versions with no answers in their entirety before reviewing the answers.” Then read the paper here, highlights first, and mark your answers against the key and its notes.

The night before, switch the filter to Watch out only and read just the red notes. They are the mistakes worth avoiding on Monday.

docs.sub: One Economist chart on crop yields, four questions, 620 words in total.
docs.lede_html:
The exam you are most likely to see again: one exhibit, four questions, points and a word cap on each. The highlights mark the words that change what is asked, the caps, and the claims in the footnote you are expected to use.

Attempt it cold on the prep page first, then read it here.

notes.label: The exhibit: actual and potential crop yield against GDP per person, both on log scales
notes.title: One chart feeds all four questions
notes.body_html:
Every 2025 question asks the same thing a new way: why does Mozambique get so much less from land as good as Germany's? The chart is small on the slide. Read it full size, highlighted, in the crop yields chart below.

Readings are approximate because both axes are log scales: potential yield ≈ $1,480 and ≈ $1,490 per hectare, actual yield ≈ $260 and ≈ $1,240.

notes.quote: political instability, corruption, and weak rule of law
notes.title: The footnote names the weak institutions Q2 wants
notes.body_html:
These are the institutions Q2 asks you to be explicit about. The key's Q2 answer reuses them almost word for word: "weak rule of law, corruption, and political instability".

Give each one a channel. Each raises the risk of investing, so farmers skip the tools, irrigation and storage that move actual yield toward potential.

notes.title: 70% is today's poverty rate, the baseline for Q4
notes.body_html: This is a share of people, so it gives Q4 its starting point. Q4 then asks about the number of people below the line in 2037, and the population keeps growing. The arithmetic sits on the Q4 poverty note.

notes.quote: nearly six times the size of Germany in terms of land per person
notes.title: Six times the land per person, and still about 24× poorer
notes.body_html: Use this fact in Q1. Mozambique has far more land per person, and the chart says that land is just as fertile. Yet Germany's GDP per person is about $29k against $1.2k. Endowments cannot explain a gap that size.

notes.quote: fertile farmland that make it an agricultural superpower
notes.title: The claim under test: good land makes a country rich
notes.body_html: The question frames resources as farmland, so the orange dots, potential yield, are the direct test: they measure what land and climate allow. If the claim held, orange would rise with income. It stays flat, about $1,600 at the poorest end and $1,900 at the richest, across incomes from about $0.4k to $60k.

notes.quote: mostly supported or mostly contradicted
notes.title: A two-way question: commit in your first words
notes.body_html: The question offers two verdicts. The key opens with one: "The chart contradicts the idea". Make Mostly contradicted your first two words. A hedge with no verdict gives away the easiest marks.

notes.quote: using specific features of the chart
notes.title: Name the chart feature, then give its number
notes.body_html: Three features carry the answer: the flat orange trend, the rising teal trend, and the two vertical lines that show each country's gap. The key cites the first by name, "The orange line is almost flat". Add the gap ratios it leaves out.

notes.quote: (8 points) Maximum 100 words
notes.title: 8 points, 100 words, about 15 minutes
notes.body_html: The prep page's time plan gives Q1 about 15 minutes: plan 5, write 10. The cap is a limit, and the key's own model answer runs to 108 words. Aim 5 to 10 words under.

notes.quote: hidden driver
notes.title: One hidden cause behind both axes
notes.body_html:
Institutions decide whether anyone invests. On farms that lifts actual yield toward potential; across the whole economy it lifts GDP per person. That is why teal rises with income while orange stays flat.

The key explains the farm side only. One sentence on the income axis is where to beat it.

notes.quote: Be explicit and specific about which types of institutions
notes.title: Name the types, one channel each
notes.body_html: "Good institutions" in general earns little. Name the types and give each a channel. The paper's own Q4 lists them: property rights, contract enforcement, open trade and logistics, finance and credit, infrastructure. The key uses rule of law, property rights, finance and open trade.

notes.quote: well established contract law doesn’t cause corn to grow
notes.title: The corn warning: no institution grows corn by itself
notes.body_html: The marker wants the middle step: institution, then investment, then yield. An answer that jumps from "rule of law" straight to "higher yields" skips what the question is testing.

notes.quote: connect your answer directly to the data shown in the chart
notes.title: Close on the gap: about 83% against under 20%
notes.body_html: End the answer back on the chart. Germany realizes about 83% of its potential yield; Mozambique realizes about 18% of equally good land. The vertical lines on the chart draw exactly this gap.

notes.quote: over 70% of employment but only about 25% of GDP
notes.title: Turn 70% of jobs and 25% of GDP into output per worker
notes.body_html:
A sector's share of GDP divided by its share of jobs gives its output per worker relative to the national average.

Mozambique farms 25 ÷ 70 ≈ 0.36 Mozambique non-farm 75 ÷ 30 = 2.5 Gap 2.5 ÷ 0.36 ≈ 7× Germany farms 1 ÷ 1 = 1.0

Room to catch up and the case for structural transformation both sit in this one fact.

notes.quote: Mozambique has a debt-to-GDP ratio of 76.9% and a CCC+ credit rating (very high default risk), compared to Germany’s 62.5% debt-to-GDP and AAA rating
notes.title: Debt ratios are close; credit ratings are far apart
notes.body_html: The debt gap is 76.9 − 62.5 = 14.4 percentage points, which is modest. The ratings are far apart: AAA is the top rating and CCC+ signals very high default risk. Lenders are pricing that risk, and it decides whether capital arrives. This fact belongs in the skeptical paragraph.

notes.quote: 2 short paragraphs, each no more than 100 words
notes.title: Two caps of 100 words, and both facts used
notes.body_html: Each paragraph has its own 100-word cap, so one cannot borrow from the other. Label them as the question does. The next sentence adds "Make sure to use both pieces of information": put the jobs fact to work in the convergence paragraph and the credit rating in the skeptical one.

notes.quote: swallow the good institutions pill
notes.title: Session 4's phrase: Vietnam's 1986 reforms
notes.body_html:
Session 4 calls Vietnam's 1986 reforms taking "the good institutions pill". Vietnam is roughly ten times richer per person since, which implies about 6% a year. Use it as the course example in the output line.

(1 + g)^40 = 10 → g ≈ 5.9% a year

notes.quote: Assume no major external shocks such as wars or pandemics
notes.title: The shocks are switched off, so do not hedge on them
notes.body_html: The paper removes the usual hedges: no wars or pandemics, normal world farm prices, unchanged climate. "It depends on shocks" earns nothing here. Each of the four forecasts has to run through the reforms: institutions and credit, investment, workers leaving farms, and who gains first.

notes.title: A count, not a rate: population keeps growing
notes.body_html:

Growth factor 1.03^10 ≈ 1.34 Count flat rate = 0.70 ÷ 1.34 ≈ 52% Count halves rate = 0.35 ÷ 1.34 ≈ 26%

"Down a lot, but less than the rate" shows you read the question.

docs.title: The 2025 exhibit: crop yields against income
docs.eyebrow: Exhibit · 2025 paper · The Economist, from Adamopoulos and Restuccia (NBER, 2018)
docs.sub: Both axes are log scales. Data for 2000.
docs.lede_html:
The chart is small on the exam slide, so here it is full size. Every number on the prep page comes from reading these dots: potential (orange) and actual (teal) yield per hectare, against GDP per person.

Say "about" for every reading. On log axes a pixel is a percentage, so a third significant digit is noise.

notes.label: Legend: teal dots actual crop yield, orange dots potential crop yield
notes.title: Orange is potential, teal is actual: easy to swap
notes.body_html:
The legend is small and sits at the top right. Orange, potential yield, is what land and climate allow, so it measures the natural resource in Q1. Teal, actual yield, is what farmers get, and capital, know-how and institutions decide it.

Swap them and every answer on the paper inverts. Check the colours before you write a word.

notes.title: The yield axis is a log scale: equal steps are equal ratios
notes.body_html:
The ticks run $50, $100, $1,000, $5,000, and each tenfold rise takes the same height. A short vertical line can hide a big ratio.

Mozambique's line looks modest, yet potential is about 5.7 times actual (1,480 ÷ 260), so it realizes only about 18%. Read values as "about" and compare by ratio, which is how the prep page reports them.

notes.title: Mozambique: land as good as Germany's, about 18% of it used
notes.body_html:
Read the two dots on Mozambique's line: potential about $1,480 a hectare, actual about $260. It gets about 18% of what its land allows, with GDP per person about $1.2k.

This vertical line is the whole 2025 paper. Q1 says the land is not the problem, Q2 explains the gap, Q3 asks whether it closes and Q4 imagines closing it.

notes.title: Germany: actual yield close to potential, about 83%

Germany's two dots almost touch: potential about $1,490, actual about $1,240, so about 83%, with GDP per person about $29k.

Germany has little room left, about 1.2×, against Mozambique's 5.7×. That is the convergence case in Q3: the Q3 key says Germany "already operates near the efficiency frontier".

notes.title: Orange trend: flat from about $1,600 to $1,900
notes.body_html:
Potential yield barely changes with income: about $1,600 a hectare at the poor end and $1,900 at the rich end, about 1.2× across a 150× range of income. The chart's own label says potential yields are not correlated with income.

This is the Q1 evidence the key cites as "The orange line is almost flat".

notes.title: Teal trend: actual yield rises about 5× with income
notes.body_html:
Actual yield climbs from about $250 a hectare at the poor end to about $1,350 at the rich end. Against the orange trend, poor countries realize about a sixth of their potential and rich ones about seven tenths.

Q2 asks for the hidden driver. Institutions make farm investment safe, and the same institutions raise GDP per person, so teal slopes up while orange stays flat.

The Q1 key says Mozambique's potential is "amongst the highest of all". These dots reach about $3,200 to $3,500 a hectare, more than twice Mozambique's ≈ $1,480, which sits just under the orange trend line (about $1,650 at its income).

docs.title: 2025 answer key: model answers and marking notes
docs.sub: Four model answers with word counts, and two marking notes on Q4.
docs.lede_html:
Read this after you have written your own answers. The yellow highlights mark what earns the points; the red ones mark where the key itself slips or where its wording sets a trap.

The key is a model to beat: on every question the prep page shows one place to do better.

notes.quote: The chart contradicts the idea that natural resource endowments explain prosperity
notes.title: The key's first sentence is the verdict
notes.body_html: The model answer settles the two-way question before any evidence. Do the same in the question's own words, "Mostly contradicted", then spend the rest on support: two chart features, then the cause.

The key reads the orange line: no built-in gap in potential between poor and rich countries. That is the direct test of the resource claim.

Add what the key leaves out: the numbers, about $1,600 to $1,900 a hectare, and the teal line rising about 5× over the same incomes.

notes.body_html:
Read off the chart, Mozambique's potential is about $1,480 a hectare and Germany's about $1,490, so "slightly higher" is within reading error. The top orange dots reach about $3,500, more than twice Mozambique's.

notes.quote: translate potential into actual productivity
notes.title: Borrow this phrase: it names the gap
notes.body_html:
"Translate potential into actual" is the chart's vertical line put into words. The key's causes follow: capital, know-how and strong institutions that support investment.

Q1 only needs the phrase and one clause of cause. Q2 is where you build the bridge in full.

notes.quote: 108 words
notes.title: The model answer breaks its own 100-word cap
notes.body_html:
The key labels its Q1 answer 108 words against a 100-word maximum; by my count the text runs to 107. Either way it is over.

Do not copy the length. The cap is a hard limit for you, and the prep page answer makes the same points in 90.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 112' role='img' aria-label='The key's 108 words against the 100 word cap, and the prep answer's 90'><text x='4' y='12' class='t-b'>Key: 108 words on a 100 cap</text><rect class='bx' x='4' y='20' width='283.6' height='18' rx='3'/><text x='145.818' y='33' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>100 allowed</text><rect class='bx-w' x='287.636' y='20' width='22.7' height='18' rx='3'/><text x='298.982' y='33' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>+8</text><text x='4' y='58' class='t-b'>Prep page answer: 90 words</text><rect class='bx-a' x='4' y='66' width='255.3' height='18' rx='3'/><text x='131.636' y='79' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>90 used</text><rect class='bx' x='259.273' y='66' width='28.4' height='18' rx='3'/><text x='273.455' y='79' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>10</text><text x='4' y='106'>Aim 5 to 10 under: trim adjectives first</text></svg>

notes.quote: strong rule of law, reliable property rights, well-functioning finance/capital markets
notes.title: Four named institutions, then their mirror image
notes.body_html:
The key names four for Germany: rule of law, property rights, finance and capital markets, and relatively open trade. For Mozambique it flips them, using the footnote's own words: weak rule of law, corruption and political instability, plus weak credit and insecure land ownership.

Naming types is what the question asks. A general "good institutions" earns little.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 118' role='img' aria-label='Institutions the key names for Germany and their opposites in Mozambique'><text x='4' y='14' class='t-b'></text><text x='130' y='14' class='t-b'>Germany</text><text x='225' y='14' class='t-b'>Mozambique</text><text x='4' y='36'>Rule of law</text><text x='130' y='36' class='t-a'>strong</text><text x='225' y='36' class='t-w'>weak</text><text x='4' y='58'>Property rights</text><text x='130' y='58' class='t-a'>reliable</text><text x='225' y='58' class='t-w'>insecure</text><text x='4' y='80'>Finance</text><text x='130' y='80' class='t-a'>works</text><text x='225' y='80' class='t-w'>weak credit</text><text x='4' y='102'>Politics, trade</text><text x='130' y='102' class='t-a'>open trade</text><text x='225' y='102' class='t-w'>instability</text><line class='ln' x1='4' y1='20' x2='316' y2='20'/></svg>

notes.quote: tractors, irrigation systems, and storage facilities
notes.title: The middle step: institutions, then investment, then yield
notes.body_html:
This is the step the question's corn warning asks for. Lower uncertainty makes farmers invest in tractors, irrigation and storage, and that capital lifts actual yield toward potential.

Without this line an answer jumps straight from rule of law to corn.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 96' role='img' aria-label='Institutions lower risk, capital follows, yield rises toward potential'><rect class='bx-a' x='4' y='8' width='90.0' height='40' rx='6'/><text x='49' y='25.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Less risk</text><text x='49' y='38.5' text-anchor='middle'>rule of law</text><line class='ln-a flow' x1='96' y1='28' x2='113' y2='28'/><path class='ln-a' d='M108.0 31.0 L113 28 L108.0 25.0'/><rect class='bx-m' x='115' y='8' width='90.0' height='40' rx='6'/><text x='160' y='25.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Capital</text><text x='160' y='38.5' text-anchor='middle'>irrigation</text><line class='ln-a' x1='207' y1='28' x2='224' y2='28'/><path class='ln-a' d='M219.0 31.0 L224 28 L219.0 25.0'/><rect class='bx-a' x='226' y='8' width='90.0' height='40' rx='6'/><text x='271' y='25.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Yield up</text><text x='271' y='38.5' text-anchor='middle'>to potential</text><text x='160' y='70' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Capital deepening on the farm</text><text x='160' y='88' text-anchor='middle'>The step the corn warning asks for</text></svg>

notes.quote: combine plots into larger, scale efficient operations
notes.title: Property rights let farms grow to an efficient size
notes.body_html:
Secure title lets a farmer buy or lease neighbouring plots and borrow against them, so farms reach a size where tractors pay. The key sets this against Mozambique's "small, fragmented plots".

Use it as the channel for property rights: one institution, one mechanism, one effect on yield.

notes.quote: Word Count: 198
notes.title: 198 of 200 words, and nothing on the income axis
notes.body_html:
The key spends its words on farms and never says why the same institutions raise GDP per person, the horizontal axis. That is why teal slopes up while orange stays flat.

One sentence on it is where to beat the key, and at 200 words it fits only if you plan.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 102' role='img' aria-label='The key explains the yield axis but not the income axis'><rect class='bx-a' x='4' y='8' width='150.0' height='42' rx='6'/><text x='79' y='26.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Yield axis</text><text x='79' y='39.5' text-anchor='middle'>key explains</text><rect class='bx-w' x='166' y='8' width='150.0' height='42' rx='6'/><text x='241' y='26.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Income axis</text><text x='241' y='39.5' text-anchor='middle'>key skips</text><text x='4' y='74'>Add: the same institutions lift all</text><text x='4' y='92'>investment, so teal rises with income</text></svg>

notes.quote: agriculture employs over 70% of workers but produces only about 25% of GDP
notes.title: The key uses the jobs fact but never turns it into a number
notes.body_html:
70% of jobs making 25% of GDP means a farm worker produces about 0.36 of the national average, and a non-farm worker about 2.5. The key calls this a "large productivity gap".

Farm 25 ÷ 70 ≈ 0.36 Non-farm 75 ÷ 30 = 2.5 Gap 2.5 ÷ 0.36 ≈ 7×

Saying about 7× is how the prep page beats the key.

notes.quote: Diminishing returns to further capital deepening
notes.title: The course concept behind the convergence paragraph
notes.body_html:
Germany "already operates near the efficiency frontier", so its next machine adds little. Mozambique's farms have almost no capital, so the first tractors and storage add a lot.

Name the concept, as the key does: diminishing returns to capital. It is the reason convergence is possible at all.

notes.diagram_caption: Illustrative curve; dashed lines show the slope at each point.

notes.quote: CCC+ credit rating severely limit
notes.title: The skeptical paragraph runs on the second fact
notes.body_html:
A CCC+ rating means expensive, scarce credit for "farmers and the government": farms cannot buy machinery, and the state cannot build irrigation, roads and storage. Germany's AAA keeps its capital cheap.

Add the prep page's point: the debt ratios are only 14.4 points apart, so debt levels alone do not explain the rating gap.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 140' role='img' aria-label='A CCC plus rating blocks both private and public investment'><rect class='bx-w' x='4' y='46' width='86.0' height='40' rx='6'/><text x='47' y='63.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>CCC+</text><text x='47' y='76.5' text-anchor='middle'>costly debt</text><rect class='bx-m' x='120' y='8' width='196.0' height='36' rx='6'/><text x='218' y='23.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Farmers</text><text x='218' y='36.5' text-anchor='middle'>no machinery</text><rect class='bx-m' x='120' y='88' width='196.0' height='36' rx='6'/><text x='218' y='103.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Government</text><text x='218' y='116.5' text-anchor='middle'>no roads, storage</text><line class='ln-w' x1='90' y1='58' x2='118' y2='28'/><path class='ln-w' d='M116.5 34.8 L118 28 L111.3 29.9'/><line class='ln-w' x1='90' y1='74' x2='118' y2='104'/><path class='ln-w' d='M111.3 102.1 L118 104 L116.5 97.2'/><text x='4' y='136' class='t-a'>Germany AAA: cheap capital continues</text></svg>

notes.quote: Word Count: 174
notes.title: Two paragraphs under two caps: 83 and 81 words
notes.body_html: The key labels both paragraphs as the question does and keeps each under its own 100-word cap. Its 174 counts the two labels too: 83 + 81 = 164 words of answer plus 10 label words. Copy the layout: two labelled paragraphs, with one supplied fact anchoring each.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 100' role='img' aria-label='The key's two Q3 paragraphs against their 100 word caps'><text x='4' y='12' class='t-b'>Words per paragraph (cap 100 each)</text><text x='4' y='34'>Convergence</text><rect class='fl-a' x='84.6' y='24' width='176.1' height='12' rx='2'/><text x='265.726' y='34' class='t-b'>83</text><text x='4' y='60'>Skeptical</text><rect class='fl-a' x='84.6' y='50' width='171.9' height='12' rx='2'/><text x='261.482' y='60' class='t-b'>81</text><line class='ln-w dash' x1='296.8' y1='18' x2='296.8' y2='76'/><text x='296.8' y='90' class='t-w' text-anchor='middle'>100</text></svg>

notes.quote: Full marks should mention “structural transformation”
notes.title: Name the concept or lose marks on line 2
notes.body_html:
The marking note is explicit: the farm jobs line needs the words "structural transformation". Workers leave low-productivity farming for industry and services, so agriculture's share of jobs falls a lot even as farm output rises.

Germany shows where it ends: about 1% of jobs on farms.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 104' role='img' aria-label='Farm share of jobs: Mozambique 70 percent, Germany 1 percent'><text x='4' y='12' class='t-b'>Farm share of jobs</text><text x='4' y='36'>Mozambique</text><rect class='bx-w' x='90' y='24' width='158.2' height='18' rx='3'/><text x='169.1' y='37' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>farm 70%</text><rect class='bx' x='248.2' y='24' width='67.8' height='18' rx='3'/><text x='4' y='64'>Germany</text><rect class='bx-w' x='90' y='52' width='2.3' height='18' rx='3'/><rect class='bx' x='92.26' y='52' width='223.7' height='18' rx='3'/><text x='204.13' y='65' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>other 99%</text><text x='4' y='96' class='t-b'>structural transformation: name it</text></svg>

notes.quote: sharply reducing extreme poverty rates
notes.title: The key answers with rates; the question asks for a count
notes.body_html:
Measure 3 is the number of people below the line, and this line of the key talks about rates. If population grows about 3% a year (the prep page's assumption; the paper gives none), it is 1.34× by 2037, and a rate that falls from 70% to 52% leaves the count unchanged.

"Down a lot" still holds if the rate falls far enough. Say the count falls less than the rate. The arithmetic is on the Q4 question note.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 96' role='img' aria-label='Count equals rate times a growing population'><rect class='bx-a' x='4' y='8' width='88.0' height='40' rx='6'/><text x='48' y='25.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>rate</text><text x='48' y='38.5' text-anchor='middle'>70% → lower</text><text x='102' y='32' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>×</text><rect class='bx-m' x='112' y='8' width='88.0' height='40' rx='6'/><text x='156' y='25.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>population</text><text x='156' y='38.5' text-anchor='middle'>× 1.34</text><text x='210' y='32' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>=</text><rect class='bx-w' x='220' y='8' width='96.0' height='40' rx='6'/><text x='268' y='25.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>count</text><text x='268' y='38.5' text-anchor='middle'>falls less</text><text x='4' y='72'>the rate must reach ≈52% just to</text><text x='4' y='90'>hold the count where it is today</text></svg>

notes.quote: Up for sure, but hard to know little or a lot
notes.title: Inequality: the key says up, with the size left open
notes.body_html:
The key does not choose between up a little and up a lot. It says up and explains why: early gains go to urban, skilled and capital-owning groups, and rural incomes catch up later.

That is the Kuznets curve, and the key says you do not have to name it for full points.

notes.diagram_caption: Illustrative curve: Mozambique on the rising side.

notes.quote: reward it (fully) if they get the reasoning correct
notes.title: "Down" also scores fully, with the right reason
notes.body_html:
Mozambique already has a high Gini coefficient and an "extractive elite". If reform lets new farm and industrial classes catch up with that elite, inequality could fall, and the key tells markers to give full marks for that reasoning.

Choose one call and argue it. The reason is what scores.

docs.title: 2024 midterm paper: Canada's trilemma and the Krugman email
docs.sub: Part 1 on two trilemma figures, part 2 on an email quoting Paul Krugman.
docs.lede_html:
The 2024 paper has two exhibits: a triangle of three outcomes Canada wants, and a family email quoting Paul Krugman on potential GDP. Part 1 asks you to explain, choose and escape; part 2 asks what potential GDP is, whether Canada is growing, and whether poor countries are stuck.

The figures on slide 2 are shown in this PDF from the prep page's copies, because the originals in the file did not convert.

notes.quote: we can’t solve for all three challenges concurrently
notes.title: The claim to explain: any two, never all three
notes.body_html: Part 1a asks you to explain the argument, not to judge it. The creator says the three goals compete, so reaching two costs the third. Your job is to show why for each pair.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 132' role='img' aria-label='Three outcomes; each pair of them costs the third'><rect class='bx' x='4' y='8' width='120.0' height='30' rx='6'/><text x='64' y='27' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>1 Population</text><rect class='bx' x='196' y='8' width='120.0' height='30' rx='6'/><text x='256' y='27' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>2 Housing</text><rect class='bx' x='100' y='96' width='120.0' height='30' rx='6'/><text x='160' y='115' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>3 Productivity</text><line class='ln-w' x1='124' y1='23' x2='196' y2='23'/><text x='160' y='17' class='t-w' text-anchor='middle'>lose 3</text><line class='ln-w' x1='64' y1='38' x2='130' y2='96'/><text x='88' y='72' class='t-w' text-anchor='end'>lose 2</text><line class='ln-w' x1='256' y1='38' x2='190' y2='96'/><text x='232' y='72' class='t-w'>lose 1</text></svg>

notes.quote: someone who knows something about Canada, but who hasn’t had your exposure to economics
notes.title: Write for a smart outsider: define every term
notes.body_html:
The audience changes the answer. Name each goal in plain words with its reason, and explain dependency ratio and productivity the first time you use them.

The key skips this setup. The prep page spends about 50 words on it and closes on the one shared constraint.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 100' role='img' aria-label='Word budget for 1a: setup, three corners, close'><text x='4' y='12' class='t-b'>Prep page plan, 290 of 300 words</text><rect class='bx-m' x='4' y='20' width='52.0' height='22' rx='3'/><text x='30' y='35' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>setup</text><text x='30' y='55' text-anchor='middle'>50</text><rect class='bx-a' x='56' y='20' width='72.8' height='22' rx='3'/><text x='92.4' y='35' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>1 + 2</text><text x='92.4' y='55' text-anchor='middle'>70</text><rect class='bx-a' x='128.8' y='20' width='72.8' height='22' rx='3'/><text x='165.2' y='35' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>1 + 3</text><text x='165.2' y='55' text-anchor='middle'>70</text><rect class='bx-a' x='201.6' y='20' width='72.8' height='22' rx='3'/><text x='238' y='35' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>2 + 3</text><text x='238' y='55' text-anchor='middle'>70</text><rect class='bx' x='274.4' y='20' width='31.2' height='22' rx='3'/><text x='290' y='35' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>end</text><text x='290' y='55' text-anchor='middle'>30</text><text x='4' y='76'>Key: 10 marks per corner, none for setup</text><text x='4' y='94'>but this reader needs the setup</text></svg>

notes.quote: we get 1+2, but not 3
notes.title: The hint gives you the structure: walk all three corners
notes.body_html:
The hint works one corner: population and housing, losing productivity. Do all three in the same form, about 70 words each.

The key does exactly that, at 10 marks a corner, and every corner fails for the same reason: homes need builders and capital that productivity also needs.

notes.quote: 30 marks
notes.title: 30 of the paper's 80 marks sit on part 1a
notes.body_html:
Part 1a is worth as much as all of Q2. The prep page's rule gives it about 28 minutes: 76 × (30 ÷ 80).

The paper does not state its time limit; the rule assumes this year's 80 minutes with 4 to read.

notes.quote: If the author is correct, which 2 outcomes would you choose
notes.title: 1b assumes the trilemma holds: pick two and own the cost
notes.body_html:
"If the author is correct" sets the premise, and the key's first grading line says answers should not fight the trilemma. Name your pair and the outcome you drop in the first sentence, then defend the drop.

Escaping the trade-off is part 1c's job. The prep page picks Option 2, the green row.

notes.quote: achieve all 3 desirable simultaneously
notes.title: 1c flips 1b: now you are asked to beat the trade-off
notes.body_html:
Part 1b forbids fighting the trilemma; part 1c asks you to defeat it. The way out is to break the assumption that links the corners: new homes must come from a slow, low-productivity sector.

The key's own preference is productivity in home building plus zoning reform.

notes.quote: Give us your best policy proposal (just one)
notes.title: One policy, made concrete, beats a list of five
notes.body_html:
The question says just one. A list spreads 200 words thin and reads as a survey. Pick one lever, then spend the words on who does what and how each corner is met.

The key grades on five criteria and rewards action words: invest, establish, create.

notes.quote: What if it’s the case that we want three outcomes for our economy, but we can only have two?
notes.title: The two figures: three outcomes and a pathway to each
notes.body_html:
Figure 1a names the three outcomes and why each matters; Figure 1b gives the pathway to each. The trade-offs come from the pathways, because each one strains another outcome.

Read them full size, highlighted: Figure 1a and Figure 1b.

notes.quote: He was talking about the US economy
notes.title: The email tells you whose economy Krugman means
notes.body_html:
Krugman was describing the US, a rich economy at the technology frontier. That line unlocks 2c: the answer to "destined to stay poor?" is no, because poor countries face a different growth problem.

The key gives 2 marks for saying exactly that.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 96' role='img' aria-label='Frontier growth against catch-up growth'><rect class='bx-w' x='4' y='6' width='150.0' height='54' rx='6'/><text x='79' y='24' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>US: frontier</text><text x='79' y='37' text-anchor='middle'>grow by inventing</text><text x='79' y='50' text-anchor='middle'>+1 point: crazy</text><rect class='bx-a' x='166' y='6' width='150.0' height='54' rx='6'/><text x='241' y='24' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Poor: catching up</text><text x='241' y='37' text-anchor='middle'>grow by adopting</text><text x='241' y='50' text-anchor='middle'>+1 point: realistic</text><text x='160' y='84' text-anchor='middle'>Vietnam: ≈6% a year since 1986</text></svg>

notes.quote: pretty much just a flat line
notes.title: A flat line of potential growth through big policy swings
notes.body_html:
Krugman's chart is potential GDP growth, the trend in capacity, which barely moved through 50 years of tax, trade and political change. Actual GDP swings with the business cycle around that trend.

That contrast is what 2a asks you to explain.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 116' role='img' aria-label='Actual GDP swings around a steady potential trend'><line class='ln-m dash' x1='20' y1='70' x2='300' y2='40'/><path class='ln-a' d='M20 70 L55 52 L90 72 L125 48 L160 68 L195 38 L230 62 L265 36 L300 42'/><text x='195' y='28' class='t-s' text-anchor='middle'>boom: above</text><text x='90' y='88' class='t-s' text-anchor='middle'>recession: below</text><text x='300' y='62' class='t-m' text-anchor='end'>potential</text><text x='4' y='108'>2a: define potential, show gaps both ways</text></svg>

notes.quote: economic growth is largely driven by innovation
notes.title: True at the frontier: there, growth means new ideas
notes.body_html:
For a rich country, more capital adds little because of diminishing returns, so growth has to come from innovation, measured as total factor productivity.

Poor countries can still grow by adding capital and adopting methods that already exist. That is the hinge of the 2c answer.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 136' role='img' aria-label='The growth model: labour force growth and productivity growth'><rect class='bx' x='4' y='52' width='80.0' height='32' rx='6'/><text x='44' y='72' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>GDP growth</text><rect class='bx' x='120' y='6' width='196.0' height='30' rx='6'/><text x='218' y='25' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Labour force growth</text><rect class='bx-a' x='120' y='52' width='196.0' height='30' rx='6'/><text x='218' y='71' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Capital deepening: poor</text><rect class='bx-m' x='120' y='98' width='196.0' height='30' rx='6'/><text x='218' y='117' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Innovation (TFP): rich</text><line class='ln' x1='84' y1='68' x2='120' y2='21'/><line class='ln' x1='84' y1='68' x2='120' y2='67'/><line class='ln' x1='84' y1='68' x2='120' y2='113'/></svg>

notes.quote: raise it by one percentage point, I think that's crazy
notes.title: One point is crazy for the US, normal for catch-up
notes.body_html:
A one-point rise in US potential growth would be huge, and nobody knows the levers at the frontier. Poor countries can grow far faster when the conditions are right.

1.063^19 ≈ 3.2 1.023^19 ≈ 1.5

That gap, four points a year, is what 2c asks about.

These are total GDP growth rates, which include labour force growth, so they show the room for catch-up, not potential growth alone. Q2c rewards both channels: more workers and more output per worker.

notes.quote: total factor productivity growth has been really pretty lousy
notes.title: TFP: the growth that more workers and capital do not explain
notes.body_html:
Total factor productivity is output growth left over after counting more workers and more capital: new ideas and better methods. Krugman says it has been weak for two decades despite new technology.

For Canada, 2b's answer adds that productivity has trailed the US.

notes.quote: our GDP is quite a bit bigger now than it was before the pandemic
notes.title: Bigger GDP is not richer people
notes.body_html:
The relative is right that GDP grew, and saying yes is worth 2 of 2b's 10 marks. Then comes the but: population grew 3.2% in 2023, the fastest since 1957, while GDP per person fell 1.3% in 2023 and 1.4% in 2024.

These are Session 8 figures, published after the 2024 exam was set; the logic is the same.

notes.quote: destined to stay poor forever
notes.title: 2c: answer no, then use the growth model
notes.body_html:
The key's 15 marks: 2 for saying no, 3 for the growth model, 5 for capital deepening with diminishing returns and an example, 5 for institutions. Ten of the fifteen sit on two ideas.

Plan about 295 words to those weights, as the prep page does.

notes.title: Marks rise through the email: 5, 10, 15
notes.body_html:
2a gives 5 marks for 100 words, 2b 10 for 150, 2c 15 for 300. Three rubric items in 2a's 100 words means one or two sentences each.

Do not let the easy first question steal time from 2c.

docs.title: 2024 Figure 1a: three desirable outcomes
docs.sub: The three goals the trilemma says Canada cannot have together, each with its reason.
docs.lede_html:
Figure 1a names the goals and gives each a reason in brackets. Those reasons are the plain-language setup 1a asks for, so read them closely.

Read it with Figure 1b next to it: 1a says what Canada wants, 1b says how each is reached, and the trade-offs come from the pathways.
docs.alt: Triangle with three corners: 1 stable population growth, to achieve a healthy dependency ratio; 2 housing affordability, an economic and social good; 3 revived productivity growth, the prime determinant of our standard of living

notes.label: Corner 1: stable population growth, to achieve a healthy dependency ratio
notes.title: 1 · Population growth, for a healthy dependency ratio
notes.body_html:
The figure gives each goal its reason. Population growth matters because of the dependency ratio: people outside working age for each person in it. Canada is aging, with about 21% of people over 65, so steady immigration keeps enough workers paying for pensions and health care.

Use this reason in 1a's setup, in plain words, for the reader who has not studied economics.

notes.label: Corner 2: housing affordability, an economic and social good
notes.title: 2 · Housing affordability, an economic and social good
notes.body_html:
Figure 1a calls affordability an economic and social good. It is mostly about who can afford shelter, how the pie is shared, while the other two goals decide how big the pie is.

That difference is the prep page's case for dropping affordability in 1b: its harm can be cushioned with targeted help. If you keep it instead, say why fairness outweighs size.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 100' role='img' aria-label='Population and productivity set the size of the pie; housing sets its share'><rect class='bx-a' x='4' y='8' width='150.0' height='50' rx='6'/><text x='79' y='24' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Size of the pie</text><text x='79' y='37' text-anchor='middle'>1 Population</text><text x='79' y='50' text-anchor='middle'>3 Productivity</text><rect class='bx-m' x='166' y='8' width='150.0' height='50' rx='6'/><text x='241' y='30.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Share of the pie</text><text x='241' y='43.5' text-anchor='middle'>2 Housing</text><text x='4' y='78'>1b: the loss you can cushion</text><text x='4' y='94'>is the one to drop</text></svg>

notes.label: Corner 3: revived productivity growth, the prime determinant of our standard of living
notes.title: 3 · Productivity, the prime determinant of living standards
notes.body_html:
The figure's own words. Output per worker is the only lasting source of higher income per person; more people add to GDP but not to GDP per person.

Canada's gap is why it is on the triangle: about $21 less output per hour worked than the US, and business productivity at 73% of the US level in 2019, down from 83% in 2002.

notes.label: The triangle: the three goals as trade-offs
notes.title: The triangle is the claim: any two crowd out the third
notes.body_html:
The sides of the triangle are the trade-offs. Each pair of goals strains the third because all three draw on the same people, savings and building capacity, and new homes come from a low-productivity sector.

The trap is treating the corners as three separate problems. 1a's marks come from showing the one shared constraint behind every corner.

docs.title: 2024 Figure 1b: pathways to achieve outcomes
docs.sub: The policy that delivers each goal, in the same corner positions as Figure 1a.
docs.lede_html:
Each corner of Figure 1b is the pathway to the matching goal in Figure 1a. The trade-offs live here: each pathway strains another corner.

Read corner 2 first. Its two levers explain two of the three corners in part 1a.
docs.alt: Triangle with three corners: 1 aggressive immigration; 2 build more homes and/or cool housing demand; 3 plus investment in advanced, traded sectors

notes.label: Pathway 1: aggressive immigration
notes.title: Pathway 1, aggressive immigration, is also a housing shock
notes.body_html:
Population growth comes from immigration: in 2023 Canada's population grew 3.2%, the fastest since 1957, almost all of it through immigration. Every newcomer also needs a home, so this pathway raises housing demand at once.

That link starts two of the three corners in 1a. Name it before you walk the triangle.

notes.label: Pathway 2: build more homes and/or cool housing demand
notes.title: Pathway 2 holds two levers, and each hurts a different corner
notes.body_html:
Building more homes pulls workers and capital into construction, a low-productivity sector, so productivity suffers. Cooling demand means fewer newcomers, so population growth suffers.

Read the “and/or” carefully: it is the trilemma in one label. Whichever lever you pull for housing, you pay with goal 3 or goal 1.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 112' role='img' aria-label='The housing pathway has two levers and each hurts a different corner'><rect class='bx-m' x='90' y='6' width='140.0' height='28' rx='6'/><text x='160' y='24' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>2 Housing</text><line class='ln-w' x1='130' y1='34' x2='80' y2='58'/><path class='ln-w' d='M83.9 52.2 L80 58 L87.0 58.6'/><line class='ln-w' x1='190' y1='34' x2='240' y2='58'/><path class='ln-w' d='M233.0 58.6 L240 58 L236.1 52.2'/><rect class='bx-w' x='4' y='60' width='150.0' height='44' rx='6'/><text x='79' y='79.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Build more</text><text x='79' y='92.5' text-anchor='middle'>hurts 3 Productivity</text><rect class='bx-w' x='166' y='60' width='150.0' height='44' rx='6'/><text x='241' y='79.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Cool demand</text><text x='241' y='92.5' text-anchor='middle'>hurts 1 Population</text></svg>

notes.label: Pathway 3: investment in advanced, traded sectors
notes.title: Pathway 3 needs the same capital housing wants
notes.body_html:
Productivity comes from investment in advanced, traded sectors: machines, software and research in industries that sell abroad. Those firms compete with home building for the same savings and skilled workers.

Canada already under-invests, about 54 cents per worker for every US dollar in 2024. Diverting more into housing widens that gap, which is the key's reason corner 1 + 2 loses productivity.

notes.label: The triangle: where the three pathways collide
notes.title: 1c's way out: make building itself productive
notes.body_html:
The pathways collide because homes come from a slow sector. Part 1c asks you to break that link, and the key's own preference is productivity in residential construction plus zoning reform.

Factory-built homes on pre-zoned land serve all three goals: supply keeps pace with immigration, and construction's own output per hour rises. That is the prep page's 1c answer.

docs.title: 2024 answer key: rubrics and example answers
docs.sub: Marks per corner for 1a, grading guidance and examples for 1b and 1c, point rubrics for the email questions.
docs.lede_html:
Read this after writing your own answers to the 2024 paper. The yellow highlights mark what earns the points; the red ones mark traps, including a rubric the key mislabels.

Slides 5 to 7 and 9 to 10 are example answers written for graders: read them for the shape of the argument. Slide 2 shows the figures from the prep page's copies, because the originals in the file did not convert.

notes.quote: chronically low (and declining!) productivity sector
notes.title: The hinge of every corner: home building is a slow sector
notes.body_html:
The key's whole 1a answer turns on this phrase. Housing a growing population takes builders and capital, and residential construction is a low-productivity sector whose productivity is falling. Every worker or dollar it absorbs is one not spent raising productivity elsewhere.

State the hinge once, in plain words, then show it breaking each corner.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 106' role='img' aria-label='A fixed pool of capital and talent shifts toward housing'><text x='4' y='12' class='t-b'>Capital and talent: one fixed pool</text><text x='4' y='35' class='t-s'>today</text><rect class='bx-a' x='60' y='20' width='128.0' height='22' rx='3'/><text x='124' y='35' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>advanced</text><rect class='bx' x='188' y='20' width='128.0' height='22' rx='3'/><text x='252' y='35' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>housing</text><text x='4' y='71' class='t-s'>1 + 2</text><rect class='bx-a' x='60' y='56' width='64.0' height='22' rx='3'/><text x='92' y='71' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>adv.</text><rect class='bx-w' x='124' y='56' width='192.0' height='22' rx='3'/><text x='220' y='71' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>housing boom</text><text x='4' y='100' class='t-w'>Productivity growth stalls: corner 3 lost</text></svg>

notes.quote: high dependency ratio
notes.title: Corner 2 + 3 fails on the dependency ratio
notes.body_html:
Cut immigration to protect housing and productivity, and the workforce ages. The key spells the ratio out in brackets: fewer working people paying the taxes that support more older people. Do the same for your reader.

The key adds a political cost, deep inter-generational divisions, which is an easy extra point.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 96' role='img' aria-label='Cutting immigration ages the workforce'><rect class='bx' x='4' y='8' width='90.0' height='44' rx='6'/><text x='49' y='27.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Cut</text><text x='49' y='40.5' text-anchor='middle'>immigration</text><line class='ln-w' x1='96' y1='30' x2='113' y2='30'/><path class='ln-w' d='M108.0 33.0 L113 30 L108.0 27.0'/><rect class='bx-w' x='115' y='8' width='90.0' height='44' rx='6'/><text x='160' y='27.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Workforce</text><text x='160' y='40.5' text-anchor='middle'>ages</text><line class='ln-w' x1='207' y1='30' x2='224' y2='30'/><path class='ln-w' d='M219.0 33.0 L224 30 L219.0 27.0'/><rect class='bx-w' x='226' y='8' width='90.0' height='44' rx='6'/><text x='271' y='27.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Fewer pay</text><text x='271' y='40.5' text-anchor='middle'>for more</text><text x='4' y='80'>Canada: about 21% already over 65</text></svg>

notes.quote: (10 marks)
notes.title: 10 marks a corner: a skipped corner costs a third of 1a
notes.body_html:
The key pays 10 marks for each corner and lists nothing for the setup. Run out of words before the third corner and you lose 10 of 30, however good the first two are.

Budget about 70 words a corner, as the prep page does, and write all three corners before polishing the opening.

notes.quote: Answers should not fight the trilemma
notes.title: 1b's first grading line: do not escape the trade-off here
notes.body_html:
Arguing that Canada can have all three belongs in 1c. In 1b, take the trade-off as binding, name your pair and give reasons for the outcome you drop.

The key grades the quality of those reasons, whichever pair you pick: it wants "reasons for deprioritizing" the goal you left out.

notes.quote: offering subsidies for lower-income households
notes.title: The key's Option 2 makes the prep page's pick and cushions the cost
notes.body_html:
The example for 1 + 3 drops affordability and softens the blow with targeted policies: more supply over time and subsidies for lower-income households. That is the same argument as the prep page's 1b answer.

It also gives a reason to keep immigration that the prep answer lacks: newcomers are "not risk averse" and bring new ideas, which links population growth to innovation.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 100' role='img' aria-label='Option 2 keeps population and productivity and cushions housing'><rect class='bx-a' x='4' y='8' width='96.0' height='30' rx='6'/><text x='52' y='27' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>1 keep</text><rect class='bx-a' x='112' y='8' width='96.0' height='30' rx='6'/><text x='160' y='27' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>3 keep</text><rect class='bx-w' x='220' y='8' width='96.0' height='30' rx='6'/><text x='268' y='27' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>2 drop</text><line class='ln-a' x1='268' y1='62' x2='268' y2='40'/><path class='ln-a' d='M271.6 46.0 L268 40 L264.4 46.0'/><text x='316' y='76' class='t-a' text-anchor='end'>cushion: subsidies, supply</text><text x='4' y='94'>Admit the cost, then soften it</text></svg>

notes.quote: Both matter.
notes.title: Resolve the trilemma and be feasible: both are marked
notes.body_html:
The first criterion has two halves. A proposal that would deliver all three goals but cannot be done, or one that is easy but leaves a corner broken, earns only part of the credit.

Show each corner met in one line, then say who acts and with what money or law.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 110' role='img' aria-label='Full credit needs a proposal that works and can be done'><text x='4' y='16' class='t-b'>Solves all 3</text><text x='130' y='16' class='t-b'>Feasible</text><text x='230' y='16' class='t-b'>Credit</text><text x='4' y='36' class='t-a'>yes</text><text x='130' y='36' class='t-a'>yes</text><text x='230' y='36' class='t-a'>full</text><text x='4' y='56' class='t-w'>yes</text><text x='130' y='56' class='t-w'>no</text><text x='230' y='56' class='t-w'>partial</text><text x='4' y='76' class='t-w'>no</text><text x='130' y='76' class='t-w'>yes</text><text x='230' y='76' class='t-w'>partial</text><text x='4' y='102'>The key: “Both matter.”</text></svg>

notes.quote: invest, establish
notes.title: Actionable means verbs the Prime Minister can sign
notes.body_html:
The key rewards proposals that are more than a study or more research. A task force or a review scores low. Use verbs that commit money or law: invest, establish, create.

The prep page's answer uses three: tie transfers to zoning, fund modular plants, open an immigration stream.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 92' role='img' aria-label='Proposals that study a problem score low; ones that commit money or law score high'><rect class='bx-w' x='4' y='8' width='150.0' height='52' rx='6'/><text x='79' y='25' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Scores low</text><text x='79' y='38' text-anchor='middle'>study, research</text><text x='79' y='51' text-anchor='middle'>a task force</text><rect class='bx-a' x='166' y='8' width='150.0' height='52' rx='6'/><text x='241' y='25' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Scores high</text><text x='241' y='38' text-anchor='middle'>invest, establish</text><text x='241' y='51' text-anchor='middle'>create</text><text x='4' y='84'>Prep answer: tie, fund, open</text></svg>

notes.quote: boosting productivity in the residential construction sector
notes.title: The setter's own escape: make home building productive
notes.body_html:
The professor states his preferred way out: raise productivity in residential construction, through how we build and the rules that govern building, such as zoning and development fees. On the demand side, steer buyers away from the quarter-acre, low-density house.

Picking this lever is safe; the marks come from making it concrete. The prep page's National Factory-Built Housing Deal does that.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 96' role='img' aria-label='The hidden assumption 1c should break'><rect class='bx-w' x='4' y='8' width='312.0' height='30' rx='6'/><text x='160' y='27' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Assumption: homes come from a slow sector</text><line class='ln-w' x1='14' y1='23' x2='306' y2='23'/><line class='ln-a flow' x1='160' y1='40' x2='160' y2='58'/><path class='ln-a' d='M156.4 52.0 L160 58 L163.6 52.0'/><rect class='bx-a' x='4' y='60' width='312.0' height='30' rx='6'/><text x='160' y='79' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Supply: build faster · Demand: denser homes</text></svg>

notes.quote: modular construction, 3D printing, and prefabricated materials
notes.title: Example 1 is the prep page's answer at greater length
notes.body_html:
The key's first A answer, a National Construction Productivity Initiative, uses factory methods, harmonized codes, digital permits and a targeted immigration stream. It ends with one line per corner, under "How It Solves the Trilemma".

Copy that close. In 200 words you have room for the levers and three one-line corner checks, not for every sub-bullet on this slide.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 90' role='img' aria-label='How the key's first example meets each corner'><text x='4' y='14' class='t-b'>Corner</text><text x='110' y='14' class='t-b'>Met by</text><text x='4' y='34'>Housing</text><text x='110' y='34'>cheaper, faster building</text><text x='4' y='54'>Productivity</text><text x='110' y='54'>construction output per hour</text><text x='4' y='74'>Population</text><text x='110' y='74'>homes exist for newcomers</text></svg>

notes.quote: “capacity” and/or “long-run sustainability”
notes.title: 2a's five marks: define it, show both gaps, say why
notes.body_html:
Two marks need the words capacity or long-run sustainability in your definition. Two more need both directions of the gap. The last mark is for the why: Krugman cares about the trend that sets living standards across generations, not one year's swing.

Five marks in 100 words means one or two sentences per item.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 92' role='img' aria-label='2a's five marks: define 2, gaps 2, why 1'><text x='4' y='12' class='t-b'>2a: 5 marks, ≈95 of 100 words</text><rect class='bx-a' x='4' y='22' width='124.8' height='24' rx='3'/><text x='66.4' y='38' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>2</text><text x='66.4' y='59' text-anchor='middle'>define</text><text x='66.4' y='72' text-anchor='middle'>capacity</text><rect class='bx-a' x='128.8' y='22' width='124.8' height='24' rx='3'/><text x='191.2' y='38' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>2</text><text x='191.2' y='59' text-anchor='middle'>gap</text><text x='191.2' y='72' text-anchor='middle'>both ways</text><rect class='bx-m' x='253.6' y='22' width='62.4' height='24' rx='3'/><text x='284.8' y='38' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>1</text><text x='284.8' y='59' text-anchor='middle'>why</text><text x='284.8' y='72' text-anchor='middle'>trend</text></svg>

notes.quote: both an explanation
notes.title: Show the gap both ways: below and above potential
notes.body_html:
Most answers describe a recession, actual GDP below potential, and stop. The key wants the boom too: overtime and machines never stopped for maintenance, a pace that cannot last.

Leave out either direction and you put one of these 2 marks at risk.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 100' role='img' aria-label='Actual GDP below potential in a recession and above it in a boom'><line class='ln-m dash' x1='20' y1='50' x2='300' y2='50'/><path class='ln-a' d='M20 50 Q 90 90 160 50 T 300 50'/><text x='90' y='86' class='t-s' text-anchor='middle'>below: idle workers</text><text x='230' y='22' class='t-s' text-anchor='middle'>above: overtime</text><text x='316' y='66' class='t-m' text-anchor='end'>potential</text></svg>

notes.quote: 2 points for answering the family member’s question properly
notes.title: Say yes first: the relative is right that GDP grew
notes.body_html: Jumping straight to "but per person it fell" skips 2 easy marks. The key wants the yes, then the but: growth came almost entirely from more workers, and living standards depend on GDP per person.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 92' role='img' aria-label='2b's ten marks: yes 2, but 3, against the US 2, causes 3'><text x='4' y='12' class='t-b'>2b: 10 marks, 150 words</text><rect class='bx-w' x='4' y='20' width='62.4' height='24' rx='3'/><text x='35.2' y='36' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>2</text><text x='35.2' y='57' text-anchor='middle'>yes</text><rect class='bx-a' x='66.4' y='20' width='93.6' height='24' rx='3'/><text x='113.2' y='36' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>3</text><text x='113.2' y='57' text-anchor='middle'>but</text><rect class='bx' x='160' y='20' width='62.4' height='24' rx='3'/><text x='191.2' y='36' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>2</text><text x='191.2' y='57' text-anchor='middle'>vs US</text><rect class='bx-a' x='222.4' y='20' width='93.6' height='24' rx='3'/><text x='269.2' y='36' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>3</text><text x='269.2' y='57' text-anchor='middle'>causes</text><text x='4' y='84'>%Δ GDP ≈ %Δ people + %Δ GDP per person</text></svg>

notes.quote: driven almost completely by labour force growth
notes.title: The but: labour input grew, output per person did not
notes.body_html:
This is 3 of the 10 marks. GDP rises when more people work, but that alone makes no one richer. The key says productivity growth, seen in GDP per capita, is what drives economic well-being.

Put a number on it, as the prep page does: population up 3.2% in 2023 while GDP per person fell 1.3%.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 96' role='img' aria-label='Canada 2023: more people, less output per person'><rect class='bx-a' x='4' y='8' width='150.0' height='44' rx='6'/><text x='79' y='27.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Labour input</text><text x='79' y='40.5' text-anchor='middle'>+3.2% people</text><rect class='bx-w' x='166' y='8' width='150.0' height='44' rx='6'/><text x='241' y='27.5' class='t-b' text-anchor='middle'>Per person</text><text x='241' y='40.5' text-anchor='middle'>−1.3% in 2023</text><text x='4' y='74'>GDP rose; living standards fell</text><text x='4' y='90' class='t-s'>Canada 2023 (S8)</text></svg>

notes.quote: 3 points for explanations of Canada’s poor productivity growth
notes.title: Three marks for causes: pick from the key's six
notes.body_html:
The key lists six causes: resource dependence, weak competition, a small market, an under-developed innovation ecosystem, the pull of the US, and higher taxes. Name three or more, one clause each.

The prep page adds a number the key lacks: business investment of about 54 cents per worker for every US dollar.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 100' role='img' aria-label='The key's six causes of Canada's weak productivity growth'><text x='4' y='12' class='t-b'>The key's six causes</text><text x='4' y='34'>resource-heavy</text><text x='164' y='34'>small market</text><text x='4' y='54'>little competition</text><text x='164' y='54'>thin innovation</text><text x='4' y='74'>pull of the US</text><text x='164' y='74'>higher taxes</text><text x='4' y='96' class='t-a'>Name three or more, one clause each</text></svg>

notes.quote: Q2, Part b)
notes.title: Mislabelled: this rubric is for 2c, the third question
notes.body_html:
The key heads this slide "Q2, Part b)" a second time, but the question text and the 15 marks belong to the third email question. If you mark your own 2b against this slide, you grade it for the wrong content.

The rubric's first 2 marks are for answering no: Krugman is describing advanced economies. The prep page calls this part 2c throughout.
notes.diagram_svg: <svg class='dg' viewBox='0 0 320 96' role='img' aria-label='Which question each email rubric belongs to'><text x='4' y='14' class='t-b'>Key slide</text><text x='80' y='14' class='t-b'>Label</text><text x='190' y='14' class='t-b'>Real question</text><text x='4' y='34'>12</text><text x='80' y='34'>Q2, Part a)</text><text x='190' y='34'>2a · 5 marks</text><text x='4' y='54'>13</text><text x='80' y='54'>Q2, Part b)</text><text x='190' y='54'>2b · 10 marks</text><text x='4' y='74' class='t-w'>14</text><text x='80' y='74' class='t-w'>Q2, Part b)</text><text x='190' y='74' class='t-w'>2c · 15 marks</text></svg>

notes.quote: diminishing returns to capital
notes.title: Five marks need the term, and the class example
notes.body_html:
The key asks for the words "diminishing returns to capital" and a concrete example. The class example: a water buffalo transforms a subsistence rice farm, while an expensive tractor barely changes a Canadian wheat field.

That is why an extra point of growth is realistic for poor countries and crazy for the US.

notes.quote: 5 marks for explaining how institutional factors
notes.title: The other five: institutions collect the high returns
notes.body_html:
High returns to capital are only potential. The key's examples: contract law and property rights, public transport and energy infrastructure, public health and education. Give three or four, one line each, and say what each lets an investor or worker do.

A counterexample helps: North Korea shows catch-up never starts without them; Vietnam's 1986 reforms show it starting.

notes.quote: Institutional Environment
notes.title: The appendix model: two channels on one foundation
notes.body_html:
The key's appendix is the course growth model. GDP growth comes from labour force growth and productivity growth; productivity comes from capital deepening, labour quality and innovation. Institutions sit under all of it.

Every 2024 answer draws on it: 1a's corners, 2b's but, and the 3 marks in 2c for using the model.
